ROME: THE LAST MARCH

Seven campaigns. One road each time. The enemy does not wait for you.
Every city on this map carries a strategic value computed live from the road network — how big a crossroads it is, and how much of a chokepoint — using degree and betweenness centrality, the same measures of "who matters, and why" from Week 3 of a real network-science course. Click any city once you're in a campaign to see it for yourself. Full details below.
Every road on this map is a real Roman road, and every city's strategic value — how big a crossroads it is, how much of a chokepoint it is — is computed live from the road network rather than written in by hand. Clicking a city runs the count of roads meeting there (its degree centrality) and, over all 504 cities on the map, Brandes' algorithm to work out how often that city sits on the shortest route between two other cities (its betweenness centrality) — the same breadth-first search the game already uses to march you and the enemy across the map, just run once for every city instead of one route at a time. Both numbers are then ranked against every other city so the game can tell you a city is "busier than almost anywhere" instead of showing a bare score. These are the exact measures of "who matters, and why" covered in Week 3 of DTU's Social Graphs and Interactions course.

How this campaign works

You play a Roman sent ahead of the main force — a legionary officer, a camp scribe, a camp cook, a praetor, or a consul, drawn at random each time you start or restart a campaign, with a name and a portrait to match. Whoever you are this time, the whole theater is on the map at once and you always see exactly where the enemy is — nothing is hidden. What moves is you, and what moves against you is the enemy force named in the briefing. Both of your starting positions are also drawn fresh from a pool of plausible spots every time, so the map layout you're looking at, and the safe route through it, won't be the same twice.

Reading the map: every city is shown as a dot with its name labeled, just like the source DARE webmap. When two names would overlap at the current zoom, the less important one steps aside — but you, the enemy, both objectives, and anywhere you can march to this turn are always labeled no matter how tight the map gets. Your own objective gets a pulsing 🏁 ring so it's never in doubt which city you're actually racing toward. A blue ring means you can click that city to march there this turn. Use the theater/world toggle (top-left) or the target/grid buttons (top-right) to switch between this campaign's default zoomed-in view and the entire map. The most important thing that just happened is always posted as a banner across the top of the screen, right under the title bar — the sidebar log underneath keeps the full turn-by-turn history if you want to scroll back through it. Every road you've actually marched down stays traced on the map in a small brown trail, each stop numbered by the turn you reached it, so you can always see your own route through the theater at a glance, the way a real campaign map would mark it.

Turns and marching: you can only ever march to a city one road away — the ones ringed in blue on the map. Click one and you march there immediately, the enemy takes its real turn in response, and that's the whole turn. Click any other city, however close it looks, and nothing happens except its information showing in the panel on the right: there is no computed route, no shortest-path shortcut to a distant destination, and no way to see how many roads something is before you've actually walked there one at a time. A long march is built entirely by you, one adjacent city after another, deciding fresh each time with full knowledge of where the enemy just moved to. Routes are genuinely long: real roads that used to be a single click are broken up into their actual real waypoint towns along the way, and most campaigns now take well over a dozen real turns to complete, so crossing a theater is a real multi-turn journey made of real decisions at every single step, not one click to a destination.

The enemy moves too, using the same shortest-path search (breadth-first search, BFS) throughout: at first it marches toward its own fixed objective by the shortest route, recomputed fresh every turn, and does not know or care where you are. But it is also checking, every turn, its own BFS distance to you. Come within 6 roads of it and it abandons its march entirely, switching permanently to hunting: from then on its shortest path is recalculated against your current position instead of its old objective, every single turn, so it adapts immediately to wherever you go next. Once it's hunting you, it never goes back to its old plan. The topbar flags this in red (⚔ HUNTING YOU) the moment it happens.

Where the actual decisions are: the road network has real branching — most cities have three or more viable ways in or out, not one forced corridor, and the real waypoint towns that break up long roads are cross-linked to their neighbors on other nearby roads too, not just strung along a single dead-straight line — so the shortest way toward your objective is rarely the only sane one to actually take, and it's often not the safest. Because you're choosing every single hop yourself, that choice is entirely yours to make, turn by turn: the whole map is one connected road network, so wherever you end up, some way through to your objective always exists, and the only real cost of a detour is the turns it spends. The enemy's route is visible to you the whole time it's making its own choices for you to react to: a dashed amber line traces its live shortest-path route across the map at all times, recalculated fresh every turn from wherever it actually is — toward its objective normally, or straight at you the instant it starts hunting, when the line itself flares bright magenta and pulses faster. Watch that line shift in real time as you move, and choose a longer road that keeps you further from its path (and further than its detection radius) instead of blindly taking whichever neighbor looks fastest. Since the starting layout is randomized every game, there's no single memorized route that always works.

Sizing up a city: click any city and, below the usual facts about it, you'll see a line on its strategic value — something like "a major junction, 5 roads meeting here" followed by "a natural chokepoint: far more routes pass through here than through most cities." That isn't flavor text made up for the occasion: the first half is the city's plain road count, and the second is computed once, for all 504 cities, with Brandes' algorithm — the standard way to work out how often a city sits on the shortest route between two other cities, built on the same breadth-first search the game already uses for marching and for the enemy's route. Both numbers are then ranked against every other city on the map, which is what turns a raw count into a comparison like "far more than most" instead of a bare number. In network-science terms, these are a city's degree centrality (how many roads meet there) and betweenness centrality (how much of the province's traffic is forced through it) — the same measures of "who matters, and why" covered in Week 3 of DTU's Social Graphs and Interactions course (sunelehmann.com/socialgraphs2026-web). A high-betweenness city is worth thinking about even off the direct route: it's the kind of place a real Roman commander would garrison, because so much of the province's movement has nowhere else to go.

Winning: reach your objective city before the enemy reaches theirs, and before the enemy ever occupies the same city as you.

Losing: the enemy reaches its objective first (their goal is secured on schedule, the way it may have happened historically), the enemy catches you by ending up on your city (far more likely once it's hunting you), or you run out of turns.

Every city on this map is a real place from the Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire (DARE, dare.ht.lu.se), the academic gazetteer behind the klokantech/roman-empire map project; 494 of the 504 cities use DARE's own surveyed coordinates directly, and the rest (a lake, a mountain pass, a river crossing, a stretch of open border country) are reconstructed because DARE doesn't carry a point for them. 398 of those 504 are waypoint towns added on top of the historical hub cities: 208 string out the longer roads between hubs, and a further 190 are real nearby places branched in specifically wherever a stretch would otherwise have been a forced single-file corridor with nothing else around to cross-link to — each one kept a real distance from its neighbors so the map stays readable rather than cluttered.

Roads work the same way: where DARE's own road-segment data (roads_low.geojson from that project) actually links two cities, this map draws that real, attested road, traced point for point. Where no single attested segment connects two cities directly — a common gap, since DARE only records roads that have actually been surveyed or excavated, not a hypothetical complete network — the map falls back to a dashed straight line between them, clearly marked as reconstructed rather than attested. Hover any road to see which kind it is. 618 of this map's 903 roads are directly attested; 285 are reconstructed gaps.
